title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
🤔 Your power analysis assumed 15 clients per practice. What happens to the power when some practices recruit 5 clients and others 30?
Before a study starts, the researcher has to decide how many participants to include, aiming to give the study a sufficiently high probability of detecting an effect, if that effect really exists. The researcher sets this probability - the statistical power - in advance, often at 80%. In practice, power analysis is used for this: a calculation based on a series of educated guesses or assumptions about what the data will look like, such as the expected size of the effect. The researcher has to make these assumptions before any data are collected. When those assumptions turn out to be wrong, the study can end up with less power than the researcher intended, and therefore with a larger risk of missing an effect that does exist.
In many studies, the researcher does not recruit participants one by one but through groups. A clinical psychologist recruits clients through psychology practices, an educational researcher recruits pupils through schools, and a medical researcher recruits patients through hospitals. The data from such studies are clustered (or multilevel or nested) data, with the groups being clusters. Clustered data occur in many kinds of studies. This post focuses on trials in which the researcher randomizes whole clusters instead of individual participants. All participants within a cluster then are assigned to the same condition and receive the same intervention or treatment. Such trials are called cluster-randomized trials. Whether the researcher randomizes clusters or individual participants, the clustering has consequences for the power analysis. The researcher then has to make additional assumptions, and one of these assumptions is the subject of this post.
When a researcher plans the sample size for a study with clustered data, the plan always contains an assumption about the number of participants in each cluster, whether the researcher makes that assumption consciously or not. To see why this assumption plays a role, consider what clustering means for a power analysis. Participants within the same cluster tend to resemble each other. Each additional participant from a cluster that is already in the study therefore contributes less than a participant from a new cluster would. A power analysis for such a trial takes this into account. The calculation therefore always assumes how the participants are spread across the clusters, even when the researcher does not choose that spread explicitly.
The simplest choice is to assume that every cluster contributes the same number of participants, usually the number the researcher expects on average. This choice is both convenient and understandable. It is convenient, because the power analysis then needs only one number. It is understandable, because the researcher often does not know in advance which clusters will recruit more and which fewer. But it has a consequence that is easy to overlook. As Part 1 of this series showed, equal clusters give the highest power that can be reached with a given number of participants. A power analysis that assumes equal clusters therefore describes the most favourable way in which the participants could be spread, and the power it reports holds only for that situation. This post examines how far the actual power can end up from the planned power when the clusters turn out to differ in size.
This post illustrates the problem with the running example of the series. A trial compares intuitive eating with structured dietary rules in adults with subclinical eating and body image concerns. Psychology practices are randomized, so all clients within a practice receive the same intervention. If clients were independent, 198 clients per arm would give 80% power to detect a standardized effect of 0.25 with a one-sided α of 0.05. Clients within the same practice tend to resemble each other. The intraclass correlation (ICC) expresses how strongly they resemble each other, as the share of the variation in body image that is due to differences between practices. With an ICC of 0.05, the trial needs more clients than that. A standard power analysis that assumes 15 clients per practice arrives at 23 practices per arm. The rest of this post calls the clusters practices and the participants clients.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
section: Why practice sizes are often hard to predict
text:
Why practice sizes are often hard to predict
A researcher who wants to plan in more detail than with one number for all practices can try to estimate for each practice how many clients it will recruit, but even a careful estimate remains uncertain. For example, the researcher can ask each practice how many eligible clients it sees, how much time its psychologists can spend on the trial, and how many referrals it expects. The researcher can also look at earlier trials in similar settings to see how recruitment was spread across sites. These estimates are made before the trial starts, however, and the circumstances on which they are based change once the trial is running. A practice loses a psychologist, its waiting list becomes longer, eligible clients decline to take part, psychologists find the trial procedures too demanding next to their regular work, a referral route disappears, or the practice withdraws after randomization. Other practices recruit more easily than expected. When the target is a total number of clients, recruitment then tends to continue in those practices until the total is reached. The sizes that result rarely match the sizes that were planned, and it is hard to know in advance how the clients will be spread across the practices.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
Unequal practices
Differences in practice size matter because clients do not all receive the same weight in the analysis. A large practice contributes more than a small one, but a practice with twice as many clients does not contribute twice as much. Because clients from the same practice resemble each other, an additional client in a large practice contributes less than an additional client in a small practice. When some practices end up larger and others smaller than planned, the extra clients in the large practices do not fully make up for the clients missing from the small practices. The total number of clients can then be exactly on target, while the power is lower than planned.








Figure 1: Each block is one client, and its height shows how much that client contributes to the comparison between the arms. Contributions are expressed in independent clients: a contribution of 8.8 means that the 15 clients of a practice together contribute as much as 8.8 clients from different practices would. Because clients from the same practice resemble each other, each additional client in a practice adds less than the previous one, so the blocks become thinner and lighter towards the top. The five clients who move from the first to the second practice (orange) contribute 1.9 in the planned situation, but only 1.4 after the move. The total contribution of the two practices therefore drops from 17.6 to 17.2, although the number of clients stays the same.





To see how much this matters, the simulation compares the planned trial, in which every practice recruits 15 clients, with trials in which the practices increasingly differ in size. In each of these trials, each arm has the planned number of practices and the planned number of clients. Both arms also have the same set of practice sizes, so that the arms differ only in the condition to which they are assigned. The simulation uses five levels of inequality. At the lowest level, the practices recruit between 8 and 23 clients. At the highest level, they recruit between 1 and 68 clients, so that a few practices provide a large share of the clients. For each trial, the simulation generates 100,000 data sets and counts how often the analysis detects the effect.
All levels of inequality can arise from the same recruitment problems. Some practices see fewer eligible clients than expected or have less time for the trial, while other practices receive more referrals than expected. How unequal the practices become depends on how large these differences are and on how many practices they affect.








Figure 2: Practice sizes in both arms of the planned trial and of the trials with increasing inequality. Each circle is one practice, and its area shows the number of clients. Within each panel, the practices are placed in random order. Every panel holds the same number of practices and the same number of clients.





Every level of inequality costs power. At the lowest level, the loss is small: 0.5 percentage points (95% Monte Carlo interval 0.3 to 0.7). It grows as the practices differ more in size, to 9.6 percentage points at the highest level, although the number of practices and the number of clients are exactly as planned. At the higher levels, many clients belong to a few large practices, where an additional client contributes less than in a small practice. The loss of power therefore depends on how the clients are spread across the practices, and it is largest when a large share of the clients ends up in a small number of practices.








Figure 3: Difference in power between the trials with unequal practices and the planned trial. The bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals. The dotted line shows the calculated difference, based on the summed contributions of the practices.











NoteSimulation details





Data were generated from a random-intercept model with an ICC of 0.05 and a standardized effect of 0.25, and analysed with a random-intercept model (nlme::lme) and a one-sided t-test on the effect of the condition. Every scenario was simulated 100,000 times. All scenarios use the same random numbers in each replication, so that the difference with the planned trial can be estimated much more precisely than the power itself. Practice sizes are fixed per scenario: they are evenly spaced quantiles of a gamma distribution with a mean of 15 clients, with a coefficient of variation of 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25 for the five levels of inequality. The calculated power uses the summed contributions of the practices and a noncentral t-distribution.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
When the arms differ
So far, both arms had the same set of practice sizes, which is unlikely in a real trial. The practices are randomized before anyone knows how many clients each practice will recruit, and sometimes even before it is clear whether the planned number of practices will be reached. The second issue returns in the next section. With a modest number of practices per arm, chance alone can place several of the larger practices in the same arm. The simulation therefore includes two further patterns. In the first pattern, one arm recruits exactly as planned, while the practices in the other arm differ in size at the same five levels as before. In the second pattern, the practices of both arms together differ in size, and the larger practices all end up in the same arm. The arms then differ not only in the sizes of their practices, but also in their number of clients. This second pattern is the least favourable result that randomization can produce.
When only one arm deviates from the plan, the loss of power is smaller than when both arms deviate (5.1 instead of 9.6 percentage points at the highest level), but it is present at every level of inequality. When the larger practices end up in the same arm, the loss grows much faster, to 26.6 percentage points at the highest level. The comparison between the arms depends on what the clients in each arm contribute together, and the arm with the smallest contribution determines most of the uncertainty about the effect. An arm that recruits as planned can therefore offset only part of a shortfall in the other arm. In the least favourable pattern, one arm consists mainly of small practices with few clients, and that arm limits the comparison.








Figure 4: Difference in power with the planned trial for the three patterns. The bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals, and the dotted lines show the calculated differences.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
When the total differs
So far, each trial reached the planned number of clients. In practice, the final number can also differ from the plan. A practice may withdraw, or it may turn out to have too few eligible clients, and such a practice cannot always be replaced. Recruitment may also stop at a fixed date before the target is reached, or continue for some time after it. The simulation therefore also includes trials with fewer clients than planned (on average 12 per practice) and trials with more clients than planned (on average 18 per practice). Each of these trials has either equal practices or practices that differ clearly in size.
When the trial recruits fewer clients than planned, the power is lower, mainly because the trial is smaller (0.75 instead of 0.80). Differences in size between the practices add to that loss (0.71). When the trial recruits more clients than planned, the power is higher than planned as long as the practices are equal (0.83). When the practices differ in size, the additional clients make up for less of the loss (0.79), and the power even ends up below the planned power. Additional clients in practices that already take part contribute less than the same number of clients in new practices would contribute, as Part 1 showed.








Figure 5: Power of the planned trial and of trials with fewer or more clients than planned, with equal practices and with practices that differ clearly in size. The bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals, and the dashed line shows the power of the planned trial.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
Taken together
A power analysis that assumes equal practices describes the most favourable situation. Every deviation from equal practices costs power, so the planned power is always an overestimation of the power that the trial actually has. How large the overestimation is depends on the deviation. When the practices differ only slightly in size, the loss is limited (0.5 percentage points in the simulation). When they differ strongly, or when the larger practices end up in the same arm, the loss is considerable (9.6 and 26.6 percentage points at the highest level). A trial can only end up above the planned power when it recruits more clients than planned, and even then differences in size between the practices reduce the gain. A small loss may seem acceptable on its own. But what is a planned power of 0.80 worth, if it is known in advance that the actual power may well be 0.78?








Figure 6: Difference in power with the planned trial for all scenarios, ordered from the smallest to the largest loss. The bars show 95% Monte Carlo intervals. Only the trials with more clients than planned can end up above zero.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
One assumption among several
A power analysis is only as good as the assumptions behind it, and the spread of the clients across the practices is only one of those assumptions. As Part 1 showed, the balance between the number of practices and the number of clients per practice is itself an assumption, and therefore a source of uncertainty as well. The ICC plays a role as well, because it determines how strongly clients from the same practice resemble each other, and therefore how much a deviation in the spread of the clients costs. A power analysis can only take this into account when the ICC is estimated well, and that is often not the case. The ICC is usually taken from earlier studies in other settings, and estimates that are based on a limited number of practices are uncertain. The expected effect size is uncertain as well, because it usually comes from earlier studies or from the difference that the researcher considers relevant. A wrong assumption about the ICC or the effect size can make the planned power too high or too low. Unequal practice sizes always make it too high. When these uncertainties come together in the same trial, the loss due to unequal practices can enlarge an overestimation of the power, or partly offset an underestimation. Which of the two happens is unknown in advance, so the researcher no longer knows where the actual power ends up.
This accumulation of uncertainties is an argument for treating the sample size from the power analysis as a starting point, which the researcher can update during the study. Designs that allow such updates are called adaptive designs. In an adaptive design, the researcher decides in advance at which moments to look at the data collected so far, and which changes to the design are allowed at those moments, such as recruiting additional participants. Sample size re-estimation is one form of this approach (see the SSR series). For the spread of the clients, it means checking during the trial whether the planned spread holds, and correcting the course when it does not. The researcher can recruit additional practices or clients, but can also support practices that fall behind, for example with a different recruitment strategy.






TipR code: power for your own practice sizes





The function below estimates the power of a cluster-randomized trial for any set of practice sizes per arm. Enter the planned sizes to check a design, or the sizes that were realized so far to see where a running trial stands.

library(nlme)

power_clusters <- function(sizes0, sizes1, icc, delta, alpha = 0.05,
                           nsim = 2000, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n    <- c(sizes0, sizes1)
  prac <- factor(rep(seq_along(n), n))
  arm  <- rep(c(0, 1), c(sum(sizes0), sum(sizes1)))
  reject <- logical(nsim)
  for (s in seq_len(nsim)) {
    y <- delta * arm + rnorm(length(n), 0, sqrt(icc))[prac] +
         rnorm(length(arm), 0, sqrt(1 - icc))
    fit <- lme(y ~ arm, random = ~ 1 | prac)
    tt  <- summary(fit)$tTable["arm", ]
    reject[s] <- tt["t-value"] > qt(1 - alpha, tt["DF"])   # one-sided
  }
  p <- mean(reject)
  c(power = p, mcse = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nsim))
}

## planned: 23 practices of 15 clients per arm
power_clusters(rep(15, 23), rep(15, 23), icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

## realized: the same number of clients, but unequal practices
sizes <- c(4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15,
           16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 25, 28, 32)
power_clusters(sizes, sizes, icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

text:
Unequal practices
Differences in practice size matter because clients do not all receive the same weight in the analysis. A large practice contributes more than a small one, but a practice with twice as many clients does not contribute twice as much. Because clients from the same practice resemble each other, an additional client in a large practice contributes less than an additional client in a small practice. When some practices end up larger and others smaller than planned, the extra clients in the large practices do not fully make up for the clients missing from the small practices. The total number of clients can then be exactly on target, while the power is lower than planned.

When the arms differ

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
When the total differs
That a trial with fewer clients than planned has less power, and a trial with more clients than planned has more power, will surprise no one. The same goes for the expected effect size. When the actual effect is larger than the researcher assumed, the power is higher than planned, and when it is smaller, the power is lower. What is less obvious is what happens when such a deviation occurs together with unequal practices. In practice, the final number of clients can easily differ from the plan. A practice may withdraw, or it may turn out to have too few eligible clients, and such a practice cannot always be replaced. Recruitment may also stop at a fixed date before the target is reached, or continue for some time after it. The simulation therefore also includes trials that recruit fewer clients than planned (on average 12 per practice) and trials that recruit more clients than planned (on average 18 per practice). Each of these trials has either equal practices or practices that differ clearly in size (CV 0.73).
When the trial recruits fewer clients than planned, the two deviations add up. With equal practices, the power drops to 0.75 because the trial is smaller, and unequal practices lower it further, to 0.71. Both deviations point in the same direction, so the shortfall in power grows. When the trial recruits more clients than planned, the deviations point in opposite directions. With equal practices, the additional clients raise the power to 0.83. Unequal practices take back part of that gain, so that the power ends up at 0.79, which is below the target power of 0.80. Additional clients can thus partly make up for unequal practices, but they only do so when the researcher happens to recruit more clients than needed. A shortfall in clients, on the other hand, always adds to the loss due to unequal practices. The same reasoning applies to the effect size. An effect that is larger than expected can hide part of the loss due to unequal practices, and an effect that is smaller than expected adds to it.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
Taken together
A power analysis that assumes equal practices describes the most favourable situation. Every deviation from equal practices costs power, so the planned power is always an overestimation of the power that the trial actually has. How large the overestimation is depends on the deviation. When the practices differ only slightly in size, the loss is limited (a power of 0.79 instead of 0.80 in the simulation). When they differ strongly, or when the larger practices end up in the same arm, the loss is considerable (a power of 0.70 and 0.53 with practices of 1 to 68 clients). A trial can only end up above the planned power when it recruits more clients than planned, and even then differences in size between the practices reduce the gain. A small loss may seem acceptable on its own. But what is a planned power of 0.80 worth, if it is known in advance that the actual power may well be 0.78?

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
One assumption among several
A power analysis is only as good as the assumptions behind it, and the spread of the clients across the practices is only one of those assumptions. As Part 1 showed, the balance between the number of practices and the number of clients per practice is itself an assumption, and therefore a source of uncertainty as well. The ICC plays a role as well, because it determines how strongly clients from the same practice resemble each other, and therefore how much a deviation in the spread of the clients costs. A power analysis can only take this into account when the ICC is estimated well, and that is often not the case. The ICC is usually taken from earlier studies in other settings, and estimates that are based on a limited number of practices are uncertain. The expected effect size is uncertain as well, because it usually comes from earlier studies or from the difference that the researcher considers relevant. A wrong assumption about the ICC or the effect size can make the planned power too high or too low. Unequal practice sizes always make it too high. When these uncertainties come together in the same trial, the loss due to unequal practices can enlarge an overestimation of the power, or partly offset an underestimation. Which of the two happens is unknown in advance, so the researcher no longer knows where the actual power ends up.
This accumulation of uncertainties is an argument for treating the sample size from the power analysis as a starting point, which the researcher can update during the study. Designs that allow such updates are called adaptive designs. In an adaptive design, the researcher decides in advance at which moments to look at the data collected so far, and which changes to the design are allowed at those moments, such as recruiting additional participants. Sample size re-estimation is one form of this approach (see the SSR series). For the spread of the clients, it means checking during the trial whether the planned spread holds, and correcting the course when it does not. The researcher can recruit additional practices or clients, but can also support practices that fall behind, for example with a different recruitment strategy.






TipR code: power for your own practice sizes





The function below estimates the power of a cluster-randomized trial for any set of practice sizes per arm. Enter the planned sizes to check a design, or the sizes that were realized so far to see where a running trial stands.

library(nlme)

power_clusters <- function(sizes0, sizes1, icc, delta, alpha = 0.05,
                           nsim = 2000, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n    <- c(sizes0, sizes1)
  prac <- factor(rep(seq_along(n), n))
  arm  <- rep(c(0, 1), c(sum(sizes0), sum(sizes1)))
  reject <- logical(nsim)
  for (s in seq_len(nsim)) {
    y <- delta * arm + rnorm(length(n), 0, sqrt(icc))[prac] +
         rnorm(length(arm), 0, sqrt(1 - icc))
    fit <- lme(y ~ arm, random = ~ 1 | prac)
    tt  <- summary(fit)$tTable["arm", ]
    reject[s] <- tt["t-value"] > qt(1 - alpha, tt["DF"])   # one-sided
  }
  p <- mean(reject)
  c(power = p, mcse = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nsim))
}

## planned: 23 practices of 15 clients per arm
power_clusters(rep(15, 23), rep(15, 23), icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

## realized: the same number of clients, but unequal practices
sizes <- c(4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15,
           16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 25, 28, 32)
power_clusters(sizes, sizes, icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

text:
When the arms differ
So far, both arms had the same set of practice sizes, which is unlikely in a real trial. The practices are randomized before anyone knows how many clients each practice will recruit, and sometimes even before it is clear whether the planned number of practices will be reached. The second issue returns in the next section. With a modest number of practices per arm, chance alone can place several of the larger practices in the same arm. The simulation therefore includes two further patterns. In the first pattern, one arm recruits exactly as planned, while the practices in the other arm differ in size at the same five levels as before. In the second pattern, the practices of both arms together differ in size, and the larger practices all end up in the same arm. The arms then differ not only in the sizes of their practices, but also in their number of clients. This second pattern is the least favourable result that randomization can produce.
When only one arm deviates from the plan, the loss of power is smaller than when both arms deviate (a power of 0.75 instead of 0.70 with practices of 1 to 68 clients), but it is present at every level of inequality. When the larger practices end up in the same arm, the power drops much further, to 0.53. The comparison between the arms depends on what the clients in each arm contribute together, and the arm with the smallest contribution determines most of the uncertainty about the effect. An arm that recruits as planned can therefore offset only part of a shortfall in the other arm. In the least favourable pattern, one arm consists mainly of small practices with few clients, and that arm limits the comparison.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
When the total differs
That a trial with fewer clients than planned has less power, and a trial with more clients than planned has more power, will surprise no one. The same goes for the expected effect size. When the actual effect is larger than the researcher assumed, the power is higher than planned, and when it is smaller, the power is lower. What is less obvious is what happens when such a deviation occurs together with unequal practices. In practice, the final number of clients can easily differ from the plan. A practice may withdraw, or it may turn out to have too few eligible clients, and such a practice cannot always be replaced. Recruitment may also stop at a fixed date before the target is reached, or continue for some time after it. The simulation therefore also includes trials that recruit fewer clients than planned (on average 12 per practice) and trials that recruit more clients than planned (on average 18 per practice). Each of these trials has either equal practices or practices that differ clearly in size (CV 0.73).
When the trial recruits fewer clients than planned, the two deviations add up. With equal practices, the power drops to 0.75 because the trial is smaller, and unequal practices lower it further, to 0.71. Both deviations point in the same direction, so the shortfall in power grows. When the trial recruits more clients than planned, the deviations point in opposite directions. With equal practices, the additional clients raise the power to 0.83. Unequal practices take back part of that gain, so that the power ends up at 0.79, which is below the target power of 0.80. Additional clients can thus partly make up for unequal practices, but they only do so when the researcher happens to recruit more clients than needed. A shortfall in clients, on the other hand, always adds to the loss due to unequal practices. The same reasoning applies to the effect size. An effect that is larger than expected can hide part of the loss due to unequal practices, and an effect that is smaller than expected adds to it.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
Taken together
A power analysis that assumes equal practices describes the most favourable situation. Every deviation from equal practices costs power, so the planned power is always an overestimation of the power that the trial actually has. How large the overestimation is depends on the deviation. When the practices differ only slightly in size, the loss is limited (a power of 0.79 instead of 0.80 in the simulation). When they differ strongly, or when the larger practices end up in the same arm, the loss is considerable (a power of 0.70 and 0.53 with practices of 1 to 68 clients). A trial can only end up above the planned power when it recruits more clients than planned, and even then differences in size between the practices reduce the gain. A small loss may seem acceptable on its own. But what is a planned power of 0.80 worth, if it is known in advance that the actual power may well be 0.78?
The literature offers corrections for this loss. Eldridge, Ashby and Kerry (2006) consider an adjustment unnecessary when the CV of the practice sizes is below 0.23. Van Breukelen, Candel and Berger (2007) find that unequal clusters rarely cost more than what about 10 percent of the clusters contribute, and propose recruiting about 11 percent more clusters to make up for it. Such corrections are practical, but they remain approximations. They need an estimate of how unequal the practices will be, which is uncertain in itself, and they assume that both arms have the same spread of practice sizes.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
One assumption among several
A power analysis is only as good as the assumptions behind it, and the spread of the clients across the practices is only one of those assumptions. As Part 1 showed, the balance between the number of practices and the number of clients per practice is itself an assumption, and therefore a source of uncertainty as well. The ICC plays a role as well, because it determines how strongly clients from the same practice resemble each other, and therefore how much a deviation in the spread of the clients costs. A power analysis can only take this into account when the ICC is estimated well, and that is often not the case. The ICC is usually taken from earlier studies in other settings, and estimates that are based on a limited number of practices are uncertain. The expected effect size is uncertain as well, because it usually comes from earlier studies or from the difference that the researcher considers relevant. A wrong assumption about the ICC or the effect size can make the planned power too high or too low. Unequal practice sizes always make it too high. When these uncertainties come together in the same trial, the loss due to unequal practices can enlarge an overestimation of the power, or partly offset an underestimation. Which of the two happens is unknown in advance, so the researcher no longer knows where the actual power ends up.
This accumulation of uncertainties is an argument for treating the sample size from the power analysis as a starting point, which the researcher can update during the study. Designs that allow such updates are called adaptive designs. In an adaptive design, the researcher decides in advance at which moments to look at the data collected so far, and which changes to the design are allowed at those moments, such as recruiting additional participants. Sample size re-estimation is one form of this approach (see the SSR series). For cluster-randomized trials, Rutterford, Copas and Eldridge (2015) describe such re-estimation of the sample size once information on the ICC and other unknown quantities becomes available during the trial, while noting that it is not yet clear at which stage these interim estimates are stable enough to rely on. For the spread of the clients, it means checking during the trial whether the planned spread holds, and correcting the course when it does not. The researcher can recruit additional practices or clients, but can also support practices that fall behind, for example with a different recruitment strategy.






TipR code: power for your own practice sizes





The function below estimates the power of a cluster-randomized trial for any set of practice sizes per arm. Enter the planned sizes to check a design, or the sizes that were realized so far to see where a running trial stands.

library(nlme)

power_clusters <- function(sizes0, sizes1, icc, delta, alpha = 0.05,
                           nsim = 2000, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n    <- c(sizes0, sizes1)
  prac <- factor(rep(seq_along(n), n))
  arm  <- rep(c(0, 1), c(sum(sizes0), sum(sizes1)))
  reject <- logical(nsim)
  for (s in seq_len(nsim)) {
    y <- delta * arm + rnorm(length(n), 0, sqrt(icc))[prac] +
         rnorm(length(arm), 0, sqrt(1 - icc))
    fit <- lme(y ~ arm, random = ~ 1 | prac)
    tt  <- summary(fit)$tTable["arm", ]
    reject[s] <- tt["t-value"] > qt(1 - alpha, tt["DF"])   # one-sided
  }
  p <- mean(reject)
  c(power = p, mcse = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nsim))
}

## planned: 23 practices of 15 clients per arm
power_clusters(rep(15, 23), rep(15, 23), icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

## realized: the same number of clients, but unequal practices
sizes <- c(4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15,
           16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 25, 28, 32)
power_clusters(sizes, sizes, icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
section: Equal clusters: the most favourable assumption
text:
Equal clusters: the most favourable assumption
When a researcher plans the sample size for a study with clustered data, the plan always contains an assumption about the number of participants in each cluster, whether the researcher makes that assumption consciously or not. To see why this assumption plays a role, consider what clustering means for a power analysis. Participants within the same cluster tend to resemble each other. As a result, each additional participant from a cluster that is already in the study contributes less than a participant from a new cluster would. A power analysis for such a trial takes this into account. The calculation thus depends on how the participants are spread across the clusters, even when the researcher does not choose that spread explicitly.
The simplest choice is to assume that every cluster contributes the same number of participants, usually the number that the researcher expects on average. This choice is both convenient and understandable. It is convenient, because the power analysis then needs only one number. It is understandable, because the researcher often does not know in advance which clusters will recruit more and which fewer. But it has a consequence that is easy to overlook. As Part 1 of this series showed, equal clusters give the highest power that can be reached with a given number of clusters and a given number of participants. A power analysis that assumes equal clusters therefore describes the most favourable way in which the participants could be spread, and the power that it reports holds only for that situation. This post examines how far the actual power can end up from the planned power when the clusters turn out to differ in size. Figure 1 shows what is at stake in the running example of this series, which the next section introduces.


Show code

  maxn <- max(unlist(rows))
  ys   <- c(2.0, 0.85)
  bx   <- 26; bw <- 8                      # power bar: x start and width of 1.0
  par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), family = "sans", xpd = TRUE)
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 36), ylim = c(0, 3.2), axes = FALSE,
       xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")

       adj = 0, cex = 0.8, col = col_dark, font = 2)
  text(bx, 2.95, "Power", adj = 0, cex = 0.8, col = col_dark, font = 2)
  set.seed(3)
  for (i in 1:2) {
    s <- rows[[i]][sample(length(rows[[i]]))]
    text(0.5, ys[i] + 0.5, labs[i], adj = 0, cex = 0.75, col = col_text)

The running example
This post illustrates the problem with the running example of the series. A trial compares intuitive eating with structured dietary rules in adults with subclinical eating and body image concerns. Psychology practices are randomized, so all clients within a practice receive the same intervention. The outcome is body image, and the researcher aims for a power of 0.80 to detect a standardized effect of 0.25 with a one-sided α of 0.05. Clients within the same practice tend to resemble each other. The intraclass correlation (ICC) expresses how strongly they resemble each other, as the share of the variation in body image that is due to differences between practices. The running example assumes an ICC of 0.05. The cards below summarize what a standard power analysis assumes for this trial and what it arrives at.


Assumed per practice
15 clients
The same number for every practice. This is the assumption that this post examines.


Without clustering, per arm
198 clients
The number of clients that would be needed if clients were independent of each other.


Planned, per arm
23 practices
With a design effect of 1 + (15 − 1) × 0.05 = 1.70, which corrects for the similarity of clients within a practice, the trial needs 337 clients per arm. Rounded up to whole practices, that is 345 clients.

text:
⚖️ Your power analysis assumed 15 clients per practice. What happens to the power when some practices recruit 5 clients and others 30?
Before a study starts, the researcher has to decide how many participants to include, aiming to give the study a sufficiently high probability of detecting an effect, if that effect really exists. The researcher sets this probability - the statistical power - in advance, often at 80%. In practice, power analysis is used for this: a calculation based on a series of educated guesses or assumptions about what the data will look like, such as the expected size of the effect. The researcher has to make these assumptions before any data are collected. When those assumptions turn out to be wrong, the study can end up with less power than the researcher intended, and therefore with a larger risk of missing an effect that does exist.
In many studies, the researcher does not recruit participants one by one but through groups. A clinical psychologist recruits clients through psychology practices, an educational researcher recruits pupils through schools, and a medical researcher recruits patients through hospitals. The data from such studies are clustered (or multilevel or nested) data, with the groups being clusters. Clustered data occur in many kinds of studies. This post focuses on trials in which the researcher randomizes whole clusters instead of individual participants. All participants within a cluster then are assigned to the same condition and receive the same intervention or treatment. Such trials are called cluster-randomized trials. Whether the researcher randomizes clusters or individual participants, the clustering has consequences for the power analysis. The researcher then has to make additional assumptions, and one of these assumptions is the subject of this post.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
section: Why practice sizes are often hard to predict
text:
Why practice sizes are often hard to predict
A researcher who wants to plan in more detail than with one number for all practices can try to estimate for each practice how many clients it will recruit, but even a careful estimate remains uncertain. For example, the researcher can ask each practice how many eligible clients it sees, how much time its psychologists can spend on the trial, and how many referrals it expects. The researcher can also look at earlier trials in similar settings to see how recruitment was spread across sites. These estimates are made before the trial starts, however, and the circumstances on which they are based change once the trial is running. A practice loses a psychologist, its waiting list becomes longer, eligible clients decline to take part, psychologists find the trial procedures too demanding next to their regular work, a referral route disappears, or the practice withdraws after randomization. Other practices recruit more easily than expected. When the target is a total number of clients, recruitment then tends to continue in those practices until the total is reached. The sizes that result rarely match the sizes that were planned, and it is hard to know in advance how the clients will be spread across the practices.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
Unequal practices
Differences in practice size matter because clients do not all receive the same weight in the analysis. A large practice contributes more than a small one, but a practice with twice as many clients does not contribute twice as much. Because clients from the same practice resemble each other, an additional client in a large practice contributes less than an additional client in a small practice. When some practices end up larger and others smaller than planned, the extra clients in the large practices do not fully make up for the clients missing from the small practices. The total number of clients can then be exactly on target, while the power is lower than planned. Part 1 described this as the contribution of a practice: all clients of a practice together contribute as much as a smaller number of clients from different practices would, and each additional client in the same practice adds a little less than the previous one. Figure 2 shows what this means when five clients move from one practice to another.








Figure 2: When five clients move from one practice to another, the number of clients stays the same, but the practices together contribute less.





In the planned situation, the five clients who later move contribute 1.9 independent clients. After the move, they contribute only 1.4, because they now join a practice that already has many clients.
How much power does this cost in the running example? To find out, we kept the number of practices and the number of clients as planned, but made the practices increasingly unequal in size. Both arms got the same set of practice sizes, so that the arms differ only in the condition to which they are assigned. We express the inequality as the coefficient of variation (CV) of the practice sizes, which the box below explains. Figure 3 shows the practice sizes that result for the running example. At a CV of 0.24, the practices recruit between 8 and 23 clients. At a CV of 1.15, they recruit between 1 and 68 clients, so that a few practices provide a large share of the clients. Such patterns can all arise from the same recruitment problems, depending on how large these problems are and on how many practices they affect.






NoteThe coefficient of variation (CV)





The coefficient of variation (CV) describes how much the practice sizes differ from each other, relative to the average practice size. Because the spread is expressed relative to the average, the same CV describes the same degree of inequality, whether the practices recruit 15 or 150 clients on average. A CV of 0 means that all practices recruit the same number of clients, and the higher the CV, the more the practice sizes differ. With an average of 15 clients per practice, a CV of 0.50 means that the practice sizes typically deviate about 7.5 clients from the average, and a CV of 1.00 means that they typically deviate about as much as the average itself. The CV is also the measure that sample size methods for unequal clusters use (Eldridge, Ashby and Kerry, 2006).
A technical detail for the interested reader: the practice sizes follow a skewed spread, with many smaller practices and a few larger ones. They were derived from skewed (gamma) distributions with a CV of 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 and 1.25, and then rounded to whole clients with at least one client per practice. This rounding makes the CV of the practice sizes that were actually used somewhat lower. The post reports these actual values.











Figure 3: The more unequal the practices, the more clients end up in a few large practices, while the number of practices and clients stays the same.





Figure 4 shows what these practice sizes mean for the power in the running example. Every level of inequality costs power, and the loss grows as the practices differ more in size.








Figure 4: In the running example, every level of inequality lowers the power below the target of 0.80, and more unequal practices lower it further.





The planned trial in Figure 4, with all practices equal, reaches a power of 0.80, close to the target of 0.80 that the power analysis aimed for. At a CV of 0.24, the power is 0.79 instead of 0.80. At a CV of 0.73, the power drops to 0.76, and at a CV of 1.15 to 0.70. In all these trials, the number of practices and the number of clients are exactly as planned. The power drops because many clients end up in a few large practices, where an additional client contributes less than in a small practice. These numbers apply to the running example, with its ICC of 0.05 and 23 practices per arm. In other trials, the loss can be smaller or larger, but the direction is the same: the more unequal the practices, the lower the power.






NoteHow the power was estimated





For each trial, we generated 100,000 data sets from a random-intercept model with an ICC of 0.05 and a standardized effect of 0.25. Each data set was analysed with a random-intercept model (nlme::lme) and a one-sided t-test on the effect of the condition. The power is the share of data sets in which this test detected the effect. All trials used the same random numbers, so that differences between the trials reflect the practice sizes and not chance.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
When the arms differ
So far, both arms had the same set of practice sizes, which is unlikely in a real trial. The practices are randomized before anyone knows how many clients each practice will recruit, and sometimes even before it is clear whether the planned number of practices will be reached. The second issue returns in the next section. With a modest number of practices per arm, chance alone can place several of the larger practices in the same arm. We therefore also looked at two other patterns. In the first pattern, one arm recruits exactly as planned, while the practices in the other arm differ in size. In the second pattern, the practices of both arms together differ in size, and the larger practices all end up in the same arm. The arms then differ not only in the sizes of their practices, but also in their number of clients. This second pattern is the least favourable result that randomization can produce.
Figure 5 compares both patterns with the trials from Figure 4. When only one arm deviates from the plan, the loss of power is smaller than when both arms deviate, but it is present at every level of inequality. When the larger practices end up in the same arm, the power drops much further.








Figure 5: One unequal arm costs less power than two, but when the larger practices end up in one arm, the power drops much further.





At the highest level of inequality, the power is 0.75 when only one arm is unequal, compared with 0.70 when both arms are unequal and 0.53 when the larger practices end up in the same arm. The comparison between the arms depends on what the clients in each arm contribute together, and the arm with the smallest contribution determines most of the uncertainty about the effect. An arm that recruits as planned can therefore offset only part of a shortfall in the other arm. In the least favourable pattern, one arm consists mainly of small practices with few clients, and that arm limits the comparison.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
When the total differs
That a trial with fewer clients than planned has less power, and a trial with more clients than planned has more power, will surprise no one. The same goes for the expected effect size. When the actual effect is larger than the researcher assumed, the power is higher than planned, and when it is smaller, the power is lower. What is less obvious is what happens when such a deviation meets unequal practices. In practice, the final number of clients can easily differ from the plan. A practice may withdraw, or it may turn out to have too few eligible clients, and such a practice cannot always be replaced. Recruitment may also stop at a fixed date before the target is reached, or continue for some time after it. Figure 6 shows what happens in the running example when the trial ends up with fewer clients than planned (on average 12 per practice) or with more (on average 18 per practice), with equal practices or with unequal practices (CV 0.73).








Figure 6: Fewer clients and unequal practices add up, while more clients can only partly make up for unequal practices.





With fewer clients than planned, the two deviations add up. With equal practices, the power drops to 0.75 because the trial is smaller, and unequal practices lower it further, to 0.71. Both deviations point in the same direction, so the shortfall in power grows. With more clients than planned, the deviations point in opposite directions. With equal practices, the additional clients raise the power to 0.83. Unequal practices take back part of that gain, so that the power ends up at 0.79, which is below the target of 0.80. Additional clients can thus partly make up for unequal practices, but only when the researcher happens to recruit more clients than needed. A shortfall in clients, on the other hand, always adds to the loss due to unequal practices. The same reasoning applies to the effect size. An effect that is larger than expected can hide part of the loss due to unequal practices, and an effect that is smaller than expected adds to it.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
Taken together
A power analysis that assumes equal practices describes the most favourable situation. In the running example, every deviation from equal practices cost power, so the planned power overestimated the power that the trial actually had. Small differences between practices cost little, but large differences cost considerably more, and the loss was largest when the larger practices ended up in the same arm. A trial could only end up above the planned power by recruiting more clients than planned, and even then unequal practices reduced the gain. A small loss may seem acceptable on its own. But what is a planned power of 0.80 worth, if it is known in advance that the actual power may well be 0.78?
The literature offers corrections for this loss. Eldridge, Ashby and Kerry (2006) consider an adjustment unnecessary when the CV of the cluster sizes is below 0.23. Van Breukelen, Candel and Berger (2007) find that unequal clusters rarely cost more than what about 10 percent of the clusters contribute, and propose recruiting about 11 percent more clusters to make up for it. Such corrections are practical, but they remain approximations. They need an estimate of how unequal the practices will be, which is uncertain in itself, and they assume that both arms have the same spread of practice sizes.

title: Sample size planning for clustered data – Part 2: When practices don’t recruit as planned
text:
One assumption among several
The spread of the clients across the practices is only one of the assumptions behind a power analysis. The ICC and the expected effect size are usually taken from earlier studies, and both are uncertain. A wrong assumption about the ICC or the effect size can make the planned power too high or too low, whereas unequal practices always make it too high. These uncertainties also interact. Guittet, Ravaud and Giraudeau (2006) showed that trials in which 80 percent of the participants belong to 20 percent of the clusters are more sensitive to a wrongly assumed ICC than trials with equal clusters. When several uncertainties come together in the same trial, the researcher no longer knows where the actual power ends up.
This accumulation of uncertainties is an argument for treating the sample size from the power analysis as a starting point, which the researcher can update during the study. Designs that allow such updates are called adaptive designs. In an adaptive design, the researcher decides in advance at which moments to look at the data collected so far, and which changes to the design are allowed at those moments, such as recruiting additional participants. Sample size re-estimation is one form of this approach (see the SSR series on the posts page). For cluster-randomized trials, Rutterford, Copas and Eldridge (2015) describe how the sample size can be re-estimated once information on the ICC and other unknown quantities becomes available during the trial, while noting that it is not yet clear at which stage these interim estimates are stable enough to rely on. For the spread of the clients, re-estimation means checking during the trial whether the planned spread holds, and correcting the course when it does not. The researcher can recruit additional practices or clients, but can also support practices that fall behind, for example with a different recruitment strategy.
Would you like to check the power for your own planned or realized practice sizes? The box below contains a short R function that does exactly that.






TipR code: power for your own practice sizes





The function below estimates the power of a cluster-randomized trial for any set of practice sizes per arm. Enter the planned sizes to check a design, or the sizes that were realized so far to see where a running trial stands.

library(nlme)

power_clusters <- function(sizes0, sizes1, icc, delta, alpha = 0.05,
                           nsim = 2000, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n    <- c(sizes0, sizes1)
  prac <- factor(rep(seq_along(n), n))
  arm  <- rep(c(0, 1), c(sum(sizes0), sum(sizes1)))
  reject <- logical(nsim)
  for (s in seq_len(nsim)) {
    y <- delta * arm + rnorm(length(n), 0, sqrt(icc))[prac] +
         rnorm(length(arm), 0, sqrt(1 - icc))
    fit <- lme(y ~ arm, random = ~ 1 | prac)
    tt  <- summary(fit)$tTable["arm", ]
    reject[s] <- tt["t-value"] > qt(1 - alpha, tt["DF"])   # one-sided
  }
  p <- mean(reject)
  c(power = p, mcse = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / nsim))
}

## planned: 23 practices of 15 clients per arm
power_clusters(rep(15, 23), rep(15, 23), icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)

## realized: the same number of clients, but unequal practices
sizes <- c(4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 15, 15,
           16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 25, 28, 32)
power_clusters(sizes, sizes, icc = 0.05, delta = 0.25)
